Current baseline prompting methods, such as Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Program-of-Thought (PoT), Chain-of-Code (CoC), and Contrastive CoT (CCoT), often yield fragmented results that lack the structural integrity needed for safety-critical IEC 61131-3 synthesis. This paper introduces CoT+ (Chain-of-Thought Extended), a unified prompting architecture that integrates these four paradigms into a deterministic, multi-stage pipeline.The novelty of this research lies in its rigorous three-layer validation framework, utilizing Human-in-the-Loop (HITL), LLM-in-the-Loop (LITL), and Bilingual Evaluation Understudy (BLEU) score analysis. To provide \"double justification\" for the superiority of CoT+, we employ an advanced Inter-Rater Reliability (IRR) assessment using Cohen\u2019s (\u03ba) for pairwise agreement and Krippendorff\u2019s (\u03b1) for multi-rater consistency. This dual-layered statistical approach ensures that performance gains are not only observable across lexical and semantic layers but are also mathematically robust and validator-agnostic. Our results demonstrate that CoT+ achieves significantly higher safety compliance and cross-validator stability than existing baselines. This research contributes: (i) a deployment-oriented prompting template for industrial PLC synthesis, and (ii) a fully reproducible,\u00a0IRR-qualified validation methodology designed for external verification in safety-critical domains.<\/jats:p>","DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6247781","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["CoT+ (Chain-of-Thought Extended): A Reproducible Multi-Reasoning Prompting Architecture for Deterministic PLC Code Generation"],"author":[{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0009-0003-1091-3313","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Ketut","family":"Adnyana","sequence":"first","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]},{"ORCID":"https:\/\/orcid.org\/0000-0001-8405-0977","authenticated-orcid":true,"given":"Andreas","family":"Schwung","sequence":"additional","affiliation":[],"role":[{"role":"author","vocabulary":"crossref"}]}],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"URL":"https:\/\/doi.org\/10.2139\/ssrn.6247781"},{"abstract":"Abstract<\/title>\n <p>Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard technique for eliciting multi-step reasoning from large language models (LLMs), and several refinements \u2014 zero-shot CoT, few-shot CoT, self-consistency decoding, and tree-of-thought (ToT) search \u2014 have each been reported to improve reasoning accuracy on frontier, closed-weight models. Comparatively little controlled evidence exists on how these strategies perform, relative to one another, on the small (3.8\u20138B parameter) open-weight instruction-tuned models that practitioners increasingly deploy for cost and privacy reasons. This paper reports a controlled empirical comparison of four CoT-based prompting strategies (zero-shot CoT, few-shot CoT, self-consistency, and tree-of-thought) across three open-weight instruction-tuned models \u2014 Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2, Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct, and Llama-3-8B-Instruct \u2014 on a 100-item subset of the GSM8K grade-school arithmetic benchmark. We report per-condition accuracy with 95% confidence intervals and test pairwise differences using McNemar's exact test on paired, per-item outcomes. Across all three models, few-shot CoT and self-consistency significantly outperform zero-shot CoT (accuracy gains of 12\u201340 percentage points, p\u2009<\u20090.05 in every model), while self-consistency with three sampled reasoning paths (k\u2009=\u20093) offers no statistically significant improvement over single-sample few-shot CoT. Tree-of-thought scores below few-shot CoT in every model (significantly so in two of three) and is statistically indistinguishable from the much cheaper zero-shot baseline in all three, despite requiring multiple sampled branches per answer. These results suggest that, for short, single-path arithmetic reasoning at this model scale, the presence of worked exemplars is the dominant driver of accuracy gains, while search-based deliberation (ToT) and low-sample self-consistency add inference cost without a corresponding, statistically reliable accuracy benefit.<\/p>","DOI":"10.21203\/rs.3.rs-11327774\/v1","type":"posted-content","is-referenced-by-count":0,"title":["Does More Deliberation Help? Consequently, their performance tends to degrade, especially when they are applied to large interconnected code bases or complex modular programs. Recently, Large Language Models (LLMs) have proven to be effective at capturing dependencies among multiple interconnected modules in the codebase. This motivated us to propose the Flow-Graph-Driven Multi-Agent Framework (FGDM), which is composed of four agents that operate in a sequential manner. The framework converts the received code to a flow graph, identifies the erroneous segments, and further generates the repaired code. All the employed agents utilize Chain-of-Thought (COT) and Tree-of-Thoughts (TOT) prompts. Additionally, we also integrated with the FAISS vector database to retrieve similar previous bugs and their repairs. We demonstrated the efficacy of the proposed framework over 100 programs from several projects, including Ansible, Black, FastAPI, Keras, Luigi, Matplotlib, Pandas, Scrapy, SpaCy, and Tornado in both C and Python programs.
